title: Raga Malar
hook: the monsoon raga opens not with rain but with what everyone forgets

segments.voice: Yesterday, Parmanand's hymn in Sarang, asking what all the listening had done, and your line was midday devotion. Did something you'd heard reach your hands at lunch? Day one thousand one hundred eighteen.

The first fat drops hit the dry street, and the smell changes before anything else does. Then the sky opens. People who were walking start running. Someone pulls laundry off a line. A child stands in the middle of the yard with her face up and her mouth open. For a few minutes, everyone stops doing what they were doing and looks up. Rain does that. The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga that tradition gives to the rainy season, called Malar. Today: Raga Malar, and how its first hymn makes everyone look up, without a drop of rain in it.
screen: `THE FIRST DROPS ON A DRY STREET.` → `EVERYONE STOPS AND LOOKS UP.` → `RAGA MALAR.`

segments.voice: Where we are: Malar follows Sarang in the Granth's order, so the book moves from the heat of midday to the rains that break the heat. Tradition calls Malar the monsoon raga and sings it in the rainy season. Its pages are full of rain pictures: clouds, thunder, the bird that cries out for a single drop. We'll hear some of those tomorrow. But here's the surprise. The section opens with a hymn of Guru Nanak that isn't about rain at all. In paraphrase: eating, drinking, laughing, sleeping, we have forgotten dying. Forgetting the Master, we've brought ourselves to ruin; a life like that won't last. Then the turn: meditate on the one Name, and go home with your honor. That's a hard first line for a rain song. Or is it? Think back to the street a minute ago. Eating, drinking, laughing, sleeping: that's the ordinary loop, and it's fine, until it carries on so smoothly that a person forgets where it ends. Then the rain comes, and for a few minutes the loop breaks, and everyone looks up. The opening of Malar does the same thing in words. It interrupts. It breaks the routine just long enough to ask what the routine has made you forget. Rain in a hot country is not gloomy. It's relief. It's what lets the fields live. And Guru Nanak's interruption, sung in the rain raga, comes the same way: a hard word about a life that won't last, and then relief, the one Name, and the way home with honor. Today's line: rain.
screen: `AFTER SARANG: THE RAINS BREAK THE HEAT.` · `EATING, DRINKING, LAUGHING, SLEEPING.` · `WE HAVE FORGOTTEN DYING.` · `RAIN INTERRUPTS, AND GIVES LIFE.` · then, large: `RAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen when it rains. If it's raining now, open a window a little and listen to it, or play a shabad sung in Malar under the sound. If it isn't, sit in the quiet and save Malar for the next rain. Either way, let this minute be an interruption. Stop the loop: no eating, no scrolling, no planning. Breathe slowly. Look up, literally, at the ceiling or the sky. Let one honest thought come about where your days are going, and don't argue with it. If you pray, you can hold Guru Nanak's line about the one Name. If you don't, simply look up. The bell holds the time.
Raga Malar. The monsoon raga that follows Sarang, sung by tradition in the rains, opening with Guru Nanak's line that in eating, drinking, laughing and sleeping we have forgotten dying. Today's word.
Your line: rain. The next time anything interrupts you today, a call, a delay, a sudden shower, use the pause to look up for one breath before you go back. Day one thousand one hundred eighteen.
